page_title: Don’t Wanna Pay Ransom Gangs? Test Your Backups.

sources.entry: Don't Wanna Pay Ransom Gangs? Test Your Backups, Krebs on Security

summary.title: Don't Wanna Pay Ransom Gangs? Test Your Backups.
summary.one_liner: Ransomware victims often pay even with backups because restore times, encrypted backup keys, corrupted backups, and missing restore tools go untested, so practice restores and plan recovery priorities in advance.
takeaways: Many victims pay ransom because they never tested how long a restore from backup would take; large backups over internet links can take months.
Backup decryption keys stored on the encrypted network leave off-site backups unusable.
Backups can occasionally be corrupted by ransomware operators, though experts say this is rarer than the other failures.
Restore software and tools may themselves be encrypted, so test restores with those dependencies in mind.
Map network dependencies, prioritize critical systems for restoration, and run periodic tabletop exercises to build and refine a ransomware playbook.
summary.summary: This Krebs on Security article explains why ransomware victims still pay for decryption keys even when they have backups. It draws on interviews with Fabian Wosar (Emsisoft) and Bill Siegel (Coveware), who name the common failures: restore times never tested, decryption keys stored on the encrypted network, corrupted backups, and restore applications that were encrypted. The article closes with advice to test restores, plan restoration order based on dependencies, and run tabletop exercises to build a recovery playbook.
